chunks: Experience in C, C++ and Python. The question: Do you have coding experience in: (these are the three most I get asked about)
The interviewer asks which of C, C++ and Python you have used. In practice, they will pick one idea from whatever you claim and test it.
So give an honest level for each language, plus one real idea you understand in each, and say which you would choose for which job.
If you have not used one, say so, and name the closest thing you have done.
Think of three tools in a workshop. C is a precise wrench: you control memory and hardware registers directly, but you can also strip a bolt.
C++ is a power-tool kit built on the same wrench, with extra safety and structure. Python is a Swiss army knife: quick for scripts and data, but wrong for hard timing jobs.
A simple decision tree. Hard real-time and register-level work points to C; big structured native projects to C++; analysis and automation to Python.
Real choices also depend on team conventions and tooling, so treat this as a starting point.
Pointer: a variable that holds a memory address.
Bit mask: a constant used with AND, OR and XOR to read or change chosen bits of a register (a hardware storage slot whose bits control a device).
volatile : a C keyword telling the compiler a value can change outside the program, such as a hardware register.
RAII: a C++ habit where an object frees its resource automatically when it goes out of scope.
Compiled vs interpreted: C and C++ are turned into the processor's own instructions before running. Python is run step by step by another program, an interpreter.
Use this skeleton, and fill the [placeholders] honestly. "In C, I have [level] experience from [microcontroller work or coursework] . In C++, [level] from [project] .
In Python, I use it for [scripting, plotting, instrument control] ." A typical concept check is a bit operation. A register holds 0x0 amps (binary 0000 1010).
reg = (1u<<2) ORs in 0000 0100, which sets bit 2 (counting from 0 at the right), giving 0x0E , which is 14. That is the whole idea.
"Yes, at different levels. C I've used on [microcontrollers or coursework] : pointers, structs, bit manipulation for registers, and volatile for ISR flags.
C++ I've used for [project] , so classes, references, RAII and the STL containers, intermediate level.
Python is what I use most, for scripting, data analysis and instrument automation.
I'd pick C for hardware-level control, Python for fast scripting and analysis, and C++ when I need abstraction with C-like performance.
Where I'm weaker, I'll say so and explain how I'd close the gap."
Quick check. In C, int a[4] = {10,20,30,40}; int p = a; What does (p + 2) evaluate to?
